rashi:a1.1: Like the size of the hole of a yoke: in which they make a hole and insert a peg to tie the straps of the yoke. Evidently a drilled hole is like a sela; so what difference is there between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel?
rashi:a1.3: And Rav Ḥisda said to him: Perhaps the drill that Beit Shammai speak of regarding the skull is “a drill and its ḥisum” that we learned. For after the hole is made, they turn the drill to the sides, take from the sides of the hole and widen it, so that the drill can enter and exit with room to spare. That is ḥisum: one removes what obstructs [ḥisem] and blocks the hole and does not let the drill enter with its full width. And a drill with its ḥisum is more than a sela.
rashi:a2.1: Rav Taḥlifa said to him, to Rav Ḥisda: Do not say “perhaps”; rather say: certainly we learned “a drill and its ḥisum.”
rashi:a2.2: And you need to rely on it: that is, you can rely on this matter.
rashi:a2.3: Like Ḥizkiyya the father of Ikkesh: whose testimony was relied upon, since no student disputed it.
rashi:a3.1: It has no backs for a distinction: its back is not distinguished from its inside. We do not say that if its back became impure, its back is impure and its inside pure; rather, if its back became impure, its inside became impure. The side that one uses is called the “inside,” even though it has no receptacle.
rashi:a4.1: And he objects: With an earthenware vessel, the Merciful One made it depend on its inside: for it becomes impure only from its inside, as it is written: “And every earthen vessel into whose inside any of them falls…”
rashi:a5.1: Its counterpart in a vessel of rinsing: that is, likewise, a vessel of rinsing that also has no inside has no [distinct] backs; and below this is explained. A vessel of rinsing is a wooden vessel, as it is written (Leviticus 15:12): “And every wooden vessel shall be rinsed in water.” And below it objects: but if it has no inside, do flat wooden vessels receive impurity? Some say a vessel of rinsing is a metal vessel, but they are mistaken: if so, why does it object below, “Do flat vessels of rinsing receive impurity?” That would be no objection, since flat metal vessels are certainly susceptible to impurity.
rashi:a7.1: This teaches us, etc.: this is why he made the vessel of rinsing depend on the earthenware vessel: where it has an inside, if its inside became impure, its back became impure.
rashi:a9.1: If it is about Torah-law impurity, indeed: for it is obvious to us that if its back became impure its inside became impure, whether it has an inside or has no inside. And here, what are we dealing with? [A case where,] with an inside, if its back became impure its inside did not become impure; and with no inside, it was necessary to teach us that if its inside became impure its back became impure, and if its back became impure its inside became impure. This is with rabbinic impurity: a vessel whose backs became impure through impure liquids.
rashi:a9.2: Its inside, its ogen: that is, the lower receptacle on which it sits. Another version: its ogen is its rim.
rashi:a9.3: Its ear: what they make on earthenware jugs as a place to grasp, which is called (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:a9.4: Its handles: such as an earthenware vessel made with a tail at its back.
rashi:a10.1: For by Torah law food and liquids do not render a vessel impure: in the first chapter of Pesaḥim (18a).
rashi:a10.2: Because of the liquid of a zav and a zava: such as his spittle and his discharge, which are a primary source of impurity and render a vessel impure by Torah law, and even a person, as it is written (Leviticus 15:8): “And if the zav spits…”
rashi:a11.1: Therefore the Rabbis made it: a vessel of rinsing that became impure through liquids.
rashi:a11.2: Like an earthenware vessel: by Torah law, where if its back became impure its inside did not become impure.
rashi:a11.3: And the Rabbis did not make it like its own Torah-law impurity, that of a vessel of rinsing: because the Rabbis made an indicator, to be lenient with the impurity of liquids, so that teruma and consecrated food would not be burned on its account, only non-sacred food. And if you ask: why did they not decree impurity of liquids on the back of an earthenware vessel? Answer: because there, there is nothing to decree on account of [the zav’s] liquid, since even if the liquid of a zav or a zava touched it from its back, it does not receive impurity; only from its inside. And if [you object] because it is written, “And an earthen vessel that the zav touches” (Leviticus 15:12), that is explained (in tractate Niddah, 42) to speak of moving it: what is “his touch” that is like all of him? You must say: this is moving it [hesset].
rashi:a14.1: And is a vessel of rinsing that has no inside susceptible to impurity by Torah law, that the Rabbis needed to decree [the impurity of] liquids on them? And further, we said above: if it is about Torah-law impurity, indeed; so there would be no need to teach us that it has no backs for a distinction.
rashi:a14.2: We require it to be like a sack: as it is written (Leviticus 11:32): “of any wooden vessel, or garment, or hide, or sack”; the wooden vessel is juxtaposed to a sack.
rashi:a14.3: Full and empty: that it has a receptacle.
rashi:a15.1: With those fit for treading: such as a chair and a bench, which receive impurity through treading.
rashi:a15.2: If so, with an earthenware vessel too: let us decree impurity on one with no inside, among those fit for treading.
rashi:a15.3: There is no treading in an earthenware vessel: for it would break if a person sat on it.
rashi:a16.1: Rav Pappa says: what you said, “You have made Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel one,” is not a refutation.
rashi:a16.2: That we learned of a large drill: in the mishna of the window made by people, it is a large drill that is like a Neronian sela. But an unspecified drill is less than a sela, and Beit Shammai speak of an unspecified drill.
rashi:a18.1: With which drill did they say: Beit Shammai, regarding the skull, “the size of a drill”: like the small one of doctors, with which they bore into the head to treat a wound.
rashi:a19.1: This works out for Rabbi Meir, etc., and further, even for Rabbi Meir, does it work out? If so, that Beit Shammai’s measure is smaller, it would be one of the leniencies of Beit Shammai. That is a leniency, since with so small a measure the skull’s impurity departs.
rashi:a19.2: And we learned six: in Eduyyot (5:1), six matters among the leniencies of Beit Shammai; seven we did not learn. [Rashi reads “and we learned six,” where the Davidson English reads “that which we learned, we learned.”]
rashi:a20.1: We learned of a Neronian sela: which is like a large drill. But the sela that Beit Hillel speak of is smaller, even than the small drill of doctors. Therefore, even according to Rabbi Meir, Beit Shammai’s measure is larger.
rashi:a21.1: Mishna. The ris of the eye: it is explained in the Gemara.
rashi:a21.2: Behold, in his eye is a dak: that is, behold, there is a dak in his eye (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:a21.3: Tevallul: it explains what it is.
rashi:a21.4: Ḥilazon [snail]: it is an illness, which is called (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:a21.5: Naḥash [snake]: it is explained in the Gemara.
rashi:a21.6: And inav [berry]: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:a21.7: A white that cuts across the sira: the sira is the ring in the eye around the black. The black is what is called (Rashi adds an Old French gloss), from which the sight of the eye comes. And if a thread of white goes out from the white, cuts across that ring and enters the black, it is a blemish.
rashi:a21.8: Black that enters the white: if a thread of black goes out from the black, cuts across the sira and enters the white.
rashi:a21.9: It is not a blemish: for there are no blemishes in the white, since it is not the eye but the fat of the eye.
tosafot:a2.1: You need to rely on it like Ḥizkiyya the father of Ikkesh: meaning, you need to take pains to settle the matter rather than declare it corrupt because of a difficulty, for it is clear to me that Shmuel said so. It is like the testimony of Ḥizkiyya the father of Ikkesh, whose wording was not settled, and [the Gemara] resolves it shortly.
tosafot:a5.1: Its counterpart in a vessel of rinsing, etc.: this term fits wooden vessels, of which it is written, “And every wooden vessel shall be rinsed in water,” as the Kuntres [Rashi] explained. But we could also say that metal vessels are likewise called vessels of rinsing, since of them it is written, “it shall be scoured and rinsed in water.” And as for what it objects below, “And is a vessel of rinsing with no inside susceptible to impurity by Torah law? We require it to be like a sack”: it is obvious to [the Gemara] that it speaks also of wooden vessels among all those called vessels of rinsing, since it did not say “metal vessels.”
tosafot:a5.2: It has no backs for a distinction; [if its inside] became impure: the side one usually uses is called its “inside.”
tosafot:a7.1: It is like an earthenware vessel: if its inside became impure, its back became impure. This must mean [its back is impure] to render other things impure, since it makes no difference for anything else. And this is difficult for the reading of Rabbeinu Shmuel in Shabbat (16a), which implies that earthenware vessels do not render impure from their backs at all. And at the end of the first chapter of Ḥullin (24a), where we say that the airspace of an earthenware vessel is impure [and its back is pure], that means it does not receive impurity from its back, but it does render others impure from its back, as is taught in Torat Kohanim: the measure for rendering impure is greater than the measure for becoming impure, for it renders others impure from its back but does not become impure from its back. Further, we say in chapter HaMappelet (Niddah 26a) that a stone protruding a handbreadth from an oven counts as a handle for conveying impurity out, and it is no better than the back. One cannot say it is better and speaks even of conveying in, for it is taught in the Tosefta that an earthenware vessel has impurity only from its airspace and by being moved. Further, we expound: “but if it has a sealed cover, it is pure,” and are we not dealing [also] with a case where he designated them for his menstruating wife? And although at the beginning of the passage of HaOr VehaRotev (Ḥullin 118a) the Talmud seems to hold that the handle of any oven serves for conveying in and out and is better than its back, in the conclusion we must say as above.
tosafot:a15.1: With those fit for treading: but other flat wooden vessels are pure; I explained their law in chapter HaMokher et HaBayit (Bava Batra 66a) and in chapter BeKhol Me’arvin (Eruvin 31a).
gershom:a2.1: Afterward he said: Perhaps this “size of a large drill” taught here, which is a sela, is “a drill and its ḥisum” that we learned: that drill with which they bore jugs, which is thin below and thick above, and that thick part blocks the hole; that is “and its ḥisum,” and that is “the size of a drill,” entering and exiting. And at any rate resolve from this the dilemma of Rabbi Oshaya [Rav Hoshaya’s question on 37b]. And Beit Shammai’s “size of a drill” regarding a skull is smaller than a sela, while Beit Hillel say “enough that if removed from a living person [he would die],” which is a sela; and this is the difference between them.
gershom:a3.1: Rav Taḥlifa said to him: You answered well, and you need to rely on it, on this answer, as we rely on the testimony of Ḥizkiyya the father of Ikkesh. That is, what you said is the main point, like that testimony of Ḥizkiyya.
gershom:a4.1: Any that has no inside, in an earthenware vessel: which has no receptacle, has no backs for a distinction; that is, its upper side is not distinguished from its lower side.
gershom:a5.1: Rather, when its inside became impure, its back became impure: that is, when one side became impure, the second side became impure.
gershom:a6.1: An earthenware vessel, when it has no inside, why does it become impure at all? The Merciful One made its impurity depend on its inside, as it is written: “And an earthen vessel into whose inside any of them falls…” If it has no inside, it does not become impure at all.
gershom:a7.1: Its counterpart in a vessel of rinsing: one that has no inside has no backs for a distinction.
gershom:a8.1: A vessel of rinsing is a metal or wooden vessel that can be purified, as it is written: “it shall be scoured and rinsed in water.”
gershom:a9.1: And how could you say so? This teaches us that one that has an inside is like an earthenware vessel, etc.
gershom:a10.1: Granted, with an earthenware vessel, the Merciful One revealed “its inside,” for the Merciful One made it depend on its inside: if its inside became impure, all of it is impure; and if not its inside but its back became impure, its inside is not impure. But a vessel of rinsing, of which “its inside” was not revealed, has no distinction.
gershom:a11.1: If it is about Torah-law impurity, such as a zav or a corpse: indeed, it has no distinction.
gershom:a12.1: Here, what are we dealing with? Rabbinic impurity of liquids, as we learned: a vessel of rinsing whose backs became impure, [that is,] its bottom.
gershom:a13.1: And it is the Rabbis who decreed: that liquids that come from a creeping animal render impure, a decree because of the liquid of a zav, which is [impure] by Torah law. Therefore, since it became impure through liquids of rabbinic law, the Rabbis made this vessel of rinsing like the impurity of an earthenware vessel, which has a distinction, and did not make it like Torah-law impurity, under which a vessel of rinsing has no distinction, whether it has an inside or not. And therefore the Rabbis made it like an earthenware vessel, so that if its back became impure its inside did not become impure, as an indicator, so that teruma and consecrated food would not be burned on its account.
gershom:a14.1: If so, one with no inside: for a vessel of rinsing, let them make for it some indicator of distinction, so that teruma and consecrated food would not be burned on its account. It is not necessary: since they made an indicator of distinction for one with an inside under rabbinic impurity, people know that when it has no inside and became impure through rabbinic liquids, one does not burn teruma and consecrated food on its account. For now that one does not burn when it has an inside, all the more so when it has no inside.
gershom:a15.1: And is a vessel of rinsing with no inside susceptible to impurity by Torah law? This is said in astonishment, as he said: with Torah-law impurity, indeed.
gershom:a16.1: But we require it to be like a sack, and since it has no inside it is not carried full and empty. [The answer:] with those vessels of rinsing that are fit for treading, for sitting, which receive Torah-law impurity even though they have no inside, as we say in tractate Shabbat, in chapter Amar Rabbi Akiva: for example, where he designated them for his menstruating wife.
gershom:a17.1: If so, an earthenware vessel too: when it has no inside, why does it not become impure, according to Rabbi Yitzḥak bar Avin? And he says: because there is no treading in an earthenware vessel, as is also explained there.
gershom:a18.1: Rav Pappa says: there is no need to answer that “we learned a drill and its ḥisum.” Rather, we learned here of a large drill, which is a sela. By inference, the unspecified drill, Beit Shammai’s, is not a large one, so it is smaller than a sela; and Beit Hillel say a sela, and their measures are not one.
gershom:a19.1: This works out for Rabbi Meir: who establishes that drill of the skull as the small drill of doctors, which is less than a sela, while Beit Hillel say a sela; that is the difference between them.
gershom:a20.1: But according to the Rabbis: who say the large one of the chamber, which is a sela, what is there to say?
gershom:a21.1: And according to Rabbi Meir: who establishes it as a small drill, it would be one of the leniencies of Beit Shammai and the stringencies of Beit Hillel. For Beit Shammai are lenient: when a little is missing, the size of a small drill, it is pure and does not impart impurity in a tent; and Beit Hillel are stringent: it never becomes pure from imparting impurity until a sela’s worth is missing. And “what we learned, we learned”: that is, they counted those six matters that are leniencies of Beit Shammai, and no more.
gershom:a22.1: Rather, Rav Naḥman answers according to Rabbi Meir’s view: we learned of a Neronian sela here, regarding a window that was made, which is like a large drill. The unspecified sela of Beit Hillel is smaller even than Beit Shammai’s unspecified drill, so Beit Hillel are on the lenient side.
gershom:a23.1: The ris of the eye: this is its eyelids.
gershom:a24.1: Behold, in his eye: as if to say, or there was a dak in his eye (Rabbeinu Gershom adds an Old French gloss).
gershom:a25.1: Ḥilazon, naḥash, inav: it is explained in the Gemara.
gershom:a26.1: That cuts across the sira and enters the black from the white: the sira is like a thread that surrounds the black.
gershom:a27.1: But if the black cuts across the sira and enters the white, it is not a blemish, for there are no blemishes in the white, since the white is not called “eye,” only the black.
rashi:b1.1: Tora bara de’eina: the outer line of the eye, that is, the eyelid that covers the eye.
rashi:b1.2: A sunken dak: a dak that sinks into the eye is a blemish.
rashi:b2.1: This in the black, that in the white: at this point [the Gemara] thinks to establish one in the black of the eye and one in the white of the eye.
rashi:b3.1: And your mnemonic is barka: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss), which is white and floating and is a blemish. So here too, let this be your sign: of a dak, a white floating one is a blemish.
rashi:b3.2: Barka: as in “one who hires a donkey and it developed barka” (Bava Metzia 78a).
rashi:b5.1: A certain elder: he was a priest.
rashi:b5.2: I did not pass before him: for he was the great one of the generation.
rashi:b5.3: This snail: that elder had a firstborn, and it had a snail in its eyes.
rashi:b7.1: Who issues a ruling of halakha: a new halakha that we have not heard from anyone else.
rashi:b7.2: Before the incident: before the incident to which the halakha applies came into his hands.
rashi:b7.3: One listens to him: and acts on it.
rashi:b7.4: One does not listen to him: since he says it on account of the incident. And here, who would heed him in what he said, that it is a permanent blemish?
rashi:b8.1: The mishna: which teaches that there is no blemish in the white is Rabbi Yosei.
rashi:b9.1: Their eyes stand forth from fatness: the wicked one went out to evil ways from the abundance of fat in his eye, and the fat of the eye is in the white.
rashi:b9.2: A thing that confuses: that cuts across the sira and mixes the black and the white; wherever it crosses, it confuses.
tosafot:b3.1: In brief: “And your mnemonic is barka” implies that barka is a permanent blemish. Tosafot asks: in Gittin (69a) there are remedies for barka, and in Shabbat (78a) we also say that one paints the eye for barkit. Answer: there it speaks of one that is just beginning, before it has set. The same answer is needed for another difficulty: in Shabbat (78a) it teaches [one is liable for carrying] blood enough to paint one eye, for so they paint for yarod (the Tosefta of Shabbat, chapter 9, has this reading), and the Tosefta of our tractate (chapter 4) writes yaor in place of ḥavarvar, which implies they are all one; and a constant ḥavarvar is counted below as a blemish. One may answer that Shabbat speaks of one that is not constant; or, alternatively, that wherever it does not heal by itself it counts as a blemish. As for what is said below of constant tears, that if they pass when the animal is fed moist and dry fodder of rain they are not constant: that is not true healing but a test of whether they are constant, while a full remedy can remove a permanent blemish. Proof: below (39b), of the gums, damaged but not removed, removal restores [the animal] to firmer health, and when merely damaged it could also be removed; though one may answer that once damaged first, it has no remedy. One might also infer from yalefet, written in the Torah and a blemish (41a), which is the Egyptian ḥazazit: Bava Kamma (80b) implies it has a remedy, since an alarm is sounded for itching on Shabbat, and that is established as the Egyptian ḥazazit, moist outside and dry inside. But one may explain that the alarm is not so that it will heal but so that it will not spread, for either way it has no remedy: we say below that it clings until the day of death, and it is written, “from which you cannot be healed.” Yet one may infer from a wart, which is written [in the Torah] and is a blemish, as below, and Eruvin (103a) teaches that one cuts off a wart in the Temple, and likewise on Passover (Pesaḥim 65b): evidently it is remedied by cutting, and it still counts as a blemish. It cannot be established as one with no bone, which is mere hanging flesh, as below; but it can be established as a wart in the eye that has no hair, for which one slaughters neither in the Temple nor in the country, even though Eruvin speaks of moist or dry, by hand or with a tool, all of which applies to a wart in the eye. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:b7.1: If he said it before the incident, one listens to him: Rabbeinu Tam says that we say this only where he needs that ruling [for himself], as here; and in Yevamot, chapter HaArel (76a), regarding “he girded a sword like Ishmael”; and in chapter Nos’in al HaAnusa (Yevamot 98a), regarding a convert marrying the wife of his maternal brother; and at the beginning of Asara Yuḥasin (Kiddushin 70b), regarding the incident of Rav Yehuda, [who said] that anyone who says “I come from the house of the Hasmoneans” is a slave, for it would have seemed that Rav Yehuda said so because the man had provoked him.
tosafot:b9.1: Their eyes stand forth from fatness: according to the exposition, the white of the eye is called fat, as the Kuntres [Rashi] explained, since the fat of the eye is there; and it means that the wicked one went out to evil ways from the abundance of fat in the eye. But the plain sense of the verse is that the eye comes out and bulges outward from the abundance of fat within it.
gershom:b1.1: Tora bara de’eina: the line outside the eye that covers the eye; this is the eyelid.
gershom:b2.1: Rather, this is a black dak and that is a white dak, as Rabba bar bar Ḥana said, etc.: this reconciles what the Sages taught with what is taught in reverse.
gershom:b3.1: And your mnemonic is barka: that is, that white dak called barka is a blemish, and that is a white dak [that floats], that is, protrudes. [A note in the printed edition supplies “that floats.”] Barka is as in “for barkit” (Shabbat 78a).
gershom:b4.1: Protruding: floating. Barak is as in “for barkit.”
gershom:b5.1: Ḥilazon is called in the vernacular (Rabbeinu Gershom adds an Old French gloss).
gershom:b6.1: Inav [berry]: that there is in his eye something like a berry, that his eye is spotted like a snake.
gershom:b7.1: This snail: he had a firstborn. [The line is garbled in the printed text; a note there suggests:] there was a dak in its eye that looked like a snail, and he said: This snail is a permanent blemish.
gershom:b8.1: And even though they said a person may not examine a blemish for himself, since the firstborn was his, he may rule for students, etc. And for that reason he called him: to teach him, so that he would permit it. And this was after the incident with his firstborn happened to him, [when] he ruled that it is a permanent blemish.
gershom:b9.1: He too was ruling from the outset: on another occasion, before the incident with his firstborn happened to him, he ruled that it is a permanent blemish. And Rabbi Meir: “a thing that confuses the eye,” whether white in the black or black in the white.
gershom:b10.1: Tarba de’eina [the fat of the eye]: that is the white in the eye.
gershom:b11.1: Ḥavarvar: if there is white in the black; and some say, a membrane.
gershom:b12.1: And constant tears: that his eyes drip constantly; this is a blemish.
gershom:b13.1: Any that lasted eighty days: and did not diminish from what it was.
gershom:b14.1: And these are constant tears: and how does one test it? If it ate moist and dry grass of rain, from a rain-fed field that drinks by itself; or ate moist and dry from an irrigated field that they water; or ate the dry of a rain field and afterward ate the moist, and still was not healed: even so it is not a blemish until it eats the dry of rain after the moist. For if it ate the moist of a rain field before the dry and was not healed by this, it is a permanent blemish. “And it lasts three months”: that is, over three months one feeds it each month moist and afterward dry.
gershom:b15.1: And how can he establish the mishna according to Rabbi Yehuda? But we learned both of them: moist and dry of rain, moist and dry of irrigation, etc.
gershom:b16.1: The matnita is incomplete, and this is what it teaches. [Rabbeinu Gershom’s wording, matnita, usually means the baraita, so he seems to apply the correction to the baraita, to bring it in line with our mishna; the Davidson English and Rashi apply it to the mishna.]
gershom:b17.1: And answer it thus: ate moist and dry of rain, it is a blemish, etc. And it accords with our mishna.
gershom:b18.1: And some say: “and it has three months,” that is, this test has three months.
gershom:b19.1: Is that so, three months and no more? Say: Adar and half of Nisan, moist; Elul and half of Adar [so the text; read: Tishrei], dry, which is three months and no more. And it teaches us that [it counts] even though they are not consecutive.
gershom:b20.1: Elul and Tishrei, dry: for at that time straw and hay are dry.
gershom:b21.1: From this, at any rate, nothing can be learned, for perhaps what he says, “Elul and Tishrei, dry,” means that we feed it the dry produce of Elul and Tishrei in Adar and Nisan.
gershom:b22.1: And how much does one feed it? Of the moist and of the dry, even a dried fig’s worth of each is enough for the test.
rashi:b10.1: Mishna. Ḥavarvar: it is an illness in which there are white drops in the eye.
rashi:b10.2: The constant: this refers to both, the ḥavarvar and the tears.
rashi:b10.3: One examines it three times within eighty days: and if they did not examine it, even though the blemish is found there on the eightieth day, it is not a blemish, for perhaps in between it went away and came back, as is its way.
rashi:b11.1: Tears: that its eyes drip water.
rashi:b11.2: These are the constant tears: that is, how do we know whether they are constant or passing?
rashi:b11.3: Ate moist and dry of rain: if they fed it, as a remedy, straw and fodder, which is called (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:b11.4: Moist: what grows in Nisan; and dry: what grows in Tishrei, as explained in the Gemara. And they fed it moist and dry of rain together, grown in a rain-fed field [beit ha-ba’al], for which rain suffices.
rashi:b11.5: Or moist and dry of irrigation: ground that needs to be watered.
rashi:b11.6: Or it did not eat moist and dry together, but ate dry and afterward ate moist as a remedy: this is not the way of remedy, so even though it was not healed by this, it is not a blemish until it eats dry after moist, for that is the way to remedy it; and if it was not healed, it is a blemish.
rashi:b12.1: Gemara. The mishna: which teaches that a constant ḥavarvar is eighty days, is Rabbi Yehuda.
rashi:b13.1: Ate moist and dry of a rain-fed field: which does not need to be watered; that is a remedy. [Rashi’s text of the baraita reads “of a rain-fed field” here, where the Davidson English reads “from an irrigated field.”]
rashi:b13.2: And not moist and dry of irrigation: which is no remedy, and we do not test with it.
rashi:b13.3: Or ate dry: of a rain-fed field, and afterward moist: it is not tested this way, for this is not the way of remedy.
rashi:b13.4: And it lasts three months: for three months we test it this way.
rashi:b14.1: But we learned both: [the mishna implies that] both of a rain-fed field and of irrigation, if it eats dry after moist, it heals, and we test with it; yet we established the mishna as Rabbi Yehuda.
rashi:b15.2: It is a blemish: if it was not healed by this.
rashi:b17.1: Moist at the time of moist: fodder that grows in Adar and Nisan, we feed it in Adar and Nisan.
rashi:b17.2: And dry at the time of dry: fodder that grows in Elul and Tishrei, we feed it in Tishrei, for they do not slaughter it until all the days of summer have passed, and it is tested with both.
rashi:b18.1: Come and hear: that it is moist at the time of moist and dry at the time of dry.
rashi:b19.1: And how much does one feed it: each day.
rashi:b19.2: At the first meal: that it eats each day, we give it a dried fig’s worth of the remedy.
